prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1, its active form and its physiological actions, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single-part B043 prize to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round showed that all six of us agree on the scientific arc, the maturity and the Drucker-Holst core, so the only open question is the third seat, and that is a question about what the citation rewards. The discovery chain is complete without the drug-development step: proglucagon processing, identification of the truncated insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36) amide, human physiology and secretion, receptor biology, and then the realisation that a stabilised agonist could be a drug. Holst, Drucker and Mojsov each hold a distinct, documented link in that chain. Outcome evidence from large randomized trials confirms the mechanism independently, so the prize would recognise an established finding and not a prospect. A one-part prize also keeps a three-person limit from being split across thinner attributions.
statement.case_against: My position is weakest on credit. Mojsov's priority relative to the Habener group, who are not among the credited names, is publicly disputed, and nothing in the material available to me lets me settle it. The committee should not hide behind that: if the primary record shows that the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) amide and the identification of the active form are mainly Habener-group findings, then naming Mojsov would be wrong and I would move to Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. Leaving out Knudsen also means a prize for the discovery side that does not name the person most associated with liraglutide and semaglutide, so some will say the therapeutic transformation goes unrecognised. And three seats cannot represent this field, so any trio will look incomplete. I also hold that this is a judgment about what a physiology or medicine citation should reward, and I could be wrong about where the line falls.

responses.point: Linnarsson prefers Drucker, Holst and Knudsen with a citation linking GLP-1 physiology to long-acting therapies, arguing that the discovery-to-therapy arc is what separates this candidate from the method-oriented ones, while saying he is not certain this is better.
responses.response: Your argument that the arc from physiology to durable drug is the distinguishing feature of B043 is fair, and it is the best case for the Knudsen seat. I still read the arc differently. The arc is why the discovery matters, but the prize credits the discovery, and the step that is hardest to replace is the identification of the active peptide and its actions. I also note that your own statement calls Mojsov's contribution contested but real. We then differ on one thing, whether translation inside a company can take a seat that otherwise goes to a discovery-level contribution. I do not think it should unless the priority record fails Mojsov. So I would ask the committee to settle priority first, and let that decide the seat rather than the framing.

responses.point: Perlmann moved from a Mojsov trio to Drucker, Holst and Knudsen because the physiology and the translation are documented and uncontested, while the priority question involves a group outside the credited names and cannot be adjudicated cleanly.
responses.response: Your move is the most considered of the round and it changes my view of the risk, though not my preference. You treat an unresolved dispute as a reason to prefer the uncontested names. That is cautious, but it also lets Mojsov's contribution lose by default and not on the evidence. My concern, as in round 1, is to state the dependence openly. If the committee cannot confirm that she contributed something decisive that Habener did not, your trio is right and I would accept it as a clean fallback. I do not accept that the translation step is uncontested in the sense that matters here, because whether industrial development belongs in the prize is exactly what we disagree on.

responses.point: El-Manira keeps Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, with Holst and Drucker as the physiology core and Knudsen as the pharmacology that made durable drugs, and warns that Habener's absence makes any trio look incomplete.
responses.response: I agree with your point on Habener, and it applies to both trios equally. If his absence makes a Mojsov trio look incomplete, it makes a Knudsen trio look incomplete as well, because the same priority question hangs over the physiology that both trios rely on. So Habener's absence cannot favour either of us. Where we differ is whether pharmacology belongs beside the physiology. Your framing is coherent and I could support it if the record on Mojsov does not hold. Where I disagree is that a three-seat prize should spend its third seat on drug development when the discovery side already has a documented claimant.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius supports Drucker, Holst and Mojsov with a citation framed around the active forms and physiology of GLP-1, but acknowledges that naming Mojsov risks crediting a disputed claim while excluding a competing one.
responses.response: We share the trio, and I share your discomfort with its most exposed point: naming Mojsov while excluding a competing claimant is only defensible if the primary record supports her. I would go further than you do in one respect. I do not think a citation worded around the active form can carry the weight of the choice. If the wording does the work, it hides the priority question and does not answer it. I would keep the citation as I have drafted it, but I would not defend the seat on the wording. I also take your point that a physiology-only citation may seem to underweight translation, and I have kept the phrase on enabling incretin-based treatment so that the clinical consequence is stated without crediting the drug-development step.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1 peptide is a contribution distinct from and not subsumed by the Habener group's work; the primary publication record has not been checked by me and I cannot settle it from the available material.

Whether a citation covering physiology only, or physiology plus drug development, should decide the third seat; I judge discovery to take precedence but I accept this is a contestable view of what the prize rewards.
Whether the omission of Habener weakens any B043 trio, and whether Knudsen's contribution should count as independent science despite its industrial setting.
For the alternatives B010 and B005, whether Ron and Kaufman should accompany Walter and Mori, and whether six optogenetics names can be reduced to three without an arbitrary choice.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my documented record for the shortlisted candidates. I have co-authored with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisen and share an institution with other members, but no credited name on the shortlist is documented as a collaborator, mentor, trainee or colleague of mine. Shared field or affiliation is not treated as a conflict. This is unchanged from round 1.
